findings.body: The query is built with an f-string that embeds `owner_id` verbatim between single quotes. Any caller-supplied value containing a quote breaks out of the string literal, so an attacker controlling `owner_id` can append arbitrary SQL (e.g. `' OR '1'='1` to read every customer's orders, or `'; DROP TABLE orders; --` to mutate data). Use a parameterized query instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A request with owner_id set to `x' OR '1'='1` makes the executed SQL `SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 'x' OR '1'='1'`, which returns every order in the table and leaks other customers' billing data.
findings.suggestion: query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
findings.title: SQL injection: owner_id interpolated directly into the query

findings.failure_scenario: When a stamped checkpoint's created_at is compared with a timezone-aware datetime (e.g. from a database or another service), Python raises TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes, breaking the comparison instead of completing it.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: Use timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) instead of utcnow()

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The new `load_order_rows` builds its SQL by f-string-interpolating `owner_id` directly into the statement text instead of using a bound parameter. Any caller-controlled value in `owner_id` becomes part of the executed SQL, so a crafted value can alter the WHERE clause or append additional statements (e.g. `' OR '1'='1` or `'; DROP TABLE orders; --`), reading or modifying rows belonging to other customers or the whole table.
findings.failure_scenario: A request supplies owner_id = "' OR customer_id <> 'x" (or a stacked-statement payload). cursor.execute runs SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '' OR customer_id <> 'x', returning every customer's order rows — cross-tenant data exposure and potential SQL injection.
findings.suggestion: cursor.execute("SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s", (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection: owner_id interpolated into query string

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time.
findings.body: `newest_queue_id`'s docstring says "Return the newest queue identifier in constant time" and "Assumes records arrive in chronological order," but the implementation performs `sorted(records, ...)` — an O(n log n) operation — and does not rely on the input being pre-sorted. The docstring makes a false claim about complexity and an irrelevant assumption, which will mislead callers and future maintainers.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer reads the docstring, assumes O(1) behavior, and calls newest_queue_id inside a hot loop over large record sets, causing an unexpected O(n log n) sort per call and a measurable performance regression.
findings.suggestion:
"""Return the identifier of the record with the latest created_at timestamp.

    Records are sorted by their created_at field, so the input does not
    need to be pre-sorted. Returns None when records is empty.
    """
findings.title: Docstring contradicts implementation: newest_queue_id is not constant-time

findings.body: `ordered[-1].get("id")` returns None when the record lacks an "id" key, and `str(None)` silently produces the string "None" rather than raising. The docstring does not document this behavior, and callers expecting a real identifier will receive the literal string "None". A docstring documenting the fallback, or an explicit error, would make the contract clear.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes records where the newest entry lacks an "id" field; the function returns the string "None", which is then persisted or used as a lookup key, silently corrupting downstream data instead of failing fast.
findings.suggestion:
"""Return the newest queue identifier, or None if records is empty.

    Raises KeyError if the newest record lacks an "id" field.
    """

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'""}, {
findings.body: The new `load_order_rows` builds the SQL statement with an f-string that interpolates `owner_id` directly into the query text (`SELECT ... WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'`). If `owner_id` originates from user input (an API path parameter, request body, or upstream record field), an attacker can terminate the string literal and append arbitrary SQL — e.g. `' OR '1'='1` to read every customer's orders, or `'; DROP TABLE orders; --` / `'; UPDATE orders SET status='shipped' WHERE '1'='1` to modify data. Even if callers currently pass trusted values, the function's signature invites unsafe use and there is no escaping or validation. Use a parameterized query so the value is bound as data, never executed as SQL.
findings.failure_scenario: A request reaches `load_order_rows` with owner_id = "x' OR '1'='1"; the f-string produces `WHERE customer_id = 'x' OR '1'='1'`, the predicate is always true, and the cursor returns every order row in the table, leaking other customers' order ids, statuses, and totals to the caller.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection: owner_id interpolated into query string
